plan.contextChunk: This figure combines a pictorial diagram with two force diagrams drawn beside it. At the left, a pulley hangs on a short stem from a beige ceiling beam; its gray grooved wheel carries a yellow cord whose two ends drop vertically to a pair of wood-grain square blocks, the higher one at the left labeled m1 and the lower one at the right labeled m2. To the right, under the headings "Block 1" and "Block 2", each block is redrawn alone as the same wood-grain square with a red vector T pointing straight up from its top edge and a red weight vector pointing straight down, labeled w1 and w2 respectively. The two tension arrows are drawn the same length, while the downward arrow on block 2 is noticeably longer than the one on block 1. Keeping the tension arrows identical while letting the weight arrows differ is the comparison the reader is meant to make. The figure sets up the Atwood machine, in which two unequal masses joined over a frictionless pulley share one string tension and accelerate equally in opposite directions.

authoredContext:
Atwood Machine A classic problem in physics, similar to the one we just solved, is that of the Atwood machine, which consists of a rope running over a pulley, with two objects of different mass attached. It is particularly useful in understanding the connection between force and motion. In the figure, m1=2.00kg and m2=4.00kg. Consider the pulley to be frictionless. (a) If m2 is released, what will its acceleration be? (b) What is the tension in the string?

T=2m1m2m1+m2g (This is found by substituting the equation for acceleration in the figure(a), into the equation for tension in the figure(b).)

An Atwood machine and free-body diagrams for each of the two blocks.

An Atwood machine consists of masses suspended on either side of a pulley by a string passing over the pulley. In the figure, mass m sub 1 is on the left and mass m sub 2 is on the right. The free body diagram of block one shows mass one with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub one pointing vertically down. The free body diagram of block two shows mass two with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub two pointing vertically down.

Strategy We draw a free-body diagram for each mass separately, as shown in the figure. Then we analyze each diagram to find the required unknowns. This may involve the solution of simultaneous equations. It is also important to note the similarity with the previous example. As block 2 accelerates with acceleration a2 in the downward direction, block 1 accelerates upward with acceleration a1. Thus, a=a1=−a2.

interactions.label: Mass of Block 2 (m2)
interactions.teaches: Changing the mass alters the downward weight vectors and the system's net acceleration, but the two upward tension vectors always remain equal to each other.

interactions.label: System State
interactions.teaches: Releasing the blocks shows that the unequal weights cause the heavier block to accelerate downward and the lighter block to accelerate upward at the exact same rate.

demo_steps.title: Static forces (Held)
demo_steps.narration: While held in place, the downward weight w2 is greater than w1. However, because they share a single string, the upward tension T is identical for both blocks.

demo_steps.title: System released
demo_steps.narration: Upon release, the imbalance in weights creates a net force. Block 2 accelerates downward while Block 1 accelerates upward. Both acceleration vectors have the same magnitude.

demo_steps.title: Reversing the mass difference
demo_steps.narration: If we make m2 lighter than m1, the net force reverses direction. The acceleration changes direction and magnitude, but the two tension arrows T remain perfectly equal to each other.

plan.keyInsight: Because the blocks are physically tied together by one continuous string, they must move together (equal acceleration) and pull on each other equally (equal tension), regardless of their individual masses.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Layout: physical pulley diagram on the left, the two free-body diagrams (FBDs) side-by-side on the right. In the FBDs, the upward tension vectors (T) MUST be drawn identically in length at all times. The downward weight vectors (w1 and w2) should scale dynamically with the mass slider. When the system state is 'released' or 'in_motion', display vertical acceleration vectors next to the FBDs that point in opposite directions but have the same length.

discrepancies: The vector arrowheads are disproportionately large compared to the original figure due to stroke-relative scaling
The vector labels in the free-body diagrams (T, w1, w2) are placed too close to the vector lines, causing them to collide with the oversized arrowheads
The mass blocks are rendered as solid tan rectangles rather than featuring the wood grain texture present in the source
The combining Unicode character used for the vector over-arrows (e.g., T⃗) renders very small and awkwardly aligned compared to the clean typesetting in the source
evaluation.notes: The physics implementation is excellent with highly pedagogical interactivity, but minor rendering artifacts like oversized arrowheads and awkward text overlaps detract from the visual polish.
action_items: Scale down the arrowhead size by adding `.attr('markerUnits', 'userSpaceOnUse')` to the `markerRed` definition, preventing the default stroke-width scaling from bloating the arrows.
Increase the horizontal offset for the left-positioned labels in `setVector` (e.g., use `labelX = x2 - 32` instead of `x2 - 22`) to clear the arrowheads.
Replace the `\u20D7` combining character with an explicitly drawn SVG line or small path over the text, as the combining character does not render reliably across browsers.
Add a simple SVG pattern fill with wavy lines for the mass blocks to emulate the wood texture seen in the source figure.

feedback.rationale: Scores are very high (overall 4.2, concept and interactivity at 5), and the noted issues are minor visual polish artifacts that do not hinder the excellent pedagogical value.
